issues.risk: A second computation of a limit anywhere else silently forks the contract; the case has to compare the enforced value against this command's output rather than against a constant.

issues.title: Make enforcement opt-in, and prove a repository that declines is unaffected
non_scope: Any default that enables enforcement
Per-command overrides; the choice is the repository's, once
issues.objective: Add one policy key that turns runtime enforcement on, default it to off, and prove with a case that a repository which never sets it behaves exactly as it does today.
issues.why: Clamping what a worker may read or emit changes how every session behaves. A change of that size cannot arrive with an update; it has to be chosen, and the choice has to be visible in the policy the repository already reviews.
issues.current_state: Nothing is enforced, so nothing needs an opt-in. Adding the adapter without one would enforce limits in every repository that updates.
issues.desired_state: The policy carries an explicit enforcement key. Absent or false, the tool behaves as it did before the adapter existed, and a case demonstrates that rather than asserting it.
acceptance_criteria: The key is declared in the policy allowlist and rejected when it holds anything but a boolean
Default and absent both mean off, and the projections say so where a worker reads them
A case runs the full lifecycle in a repository that never sets the key and shows unchanged behaviour
Doctor reports whether enforcement is on, without turning it on
issues.risk: An opt-in that defaults to on in the skeleton is not an opt-in; the skeleton has to be covered by the same case.

issues.title: Apply one derived limit for real and prove it changes what happens
non_scope: A second provider; one honest adapter first
Any provider knob whose effect cannot be observed from a test in this repository
issues.objective: Implement the first adapter: one limit, derived from the profile through the resolver, applied where a provider can honestly apply it, with a behavioural case that fails if the limit stops being applied.
issues.why: The milestone's whole distinction is between a limit that is printed and a limit that is applied. One limit that genuinely bites is worth more than a full set that is advisory, and it is the only thing that makes the claim publishable.
issues.current_state: The mapping exists, the resolver prints the numbers, and the opt-in exists. Nothing anywhere applies a value to anything.
issues.desired_state: With enforcement on, one provider's execution is constrained by a value derived from the active profile, and turning the profile from one value to another changes the observed outcome.
acceptance_criteria: The applied value comes from the resolver, and no constant appears in the adapter
A case changes only the profile and observes a different outcome
A case with enforcement off observes the unconstrained outcome
Removing the application makes a case fail rather than a document go stale
issues.risk: The only honest adapters are for knobs a provider exposes and documents; if the chosen knob turns out to be advisory on the provider's side, the issue closes as no_match rather than shipping a clamp that does not clamp.

issues.title: Declare the clamp as a doctrine so the mapping and the adapter cannot drift
non_scope: Blocking on anything a worker cannot fix from inside the repository
issues.objective: Declare the rule that every applied limit is derived from the declared mapping as a doctrine with its own validator, dispatched from the registry, reaching the command that claims to run it, covered by a case and run in CI.
issues.why: A new enforced rule that lives as an inline check inside a command is invisible to doctor and to the doctrine list, and drifts the first time somebody edits the adapter. The registry is the only place a rule can be proven to be wired.
issues.current_state: One adapter applies one derived limit. Nothing refuses an adapter that stops consulting the mapping, and nothing lists this rule among the rules the repository enforces.
issues.desired_state: The rule appears in the doctrine list, a refusal names it, doctor proves it reaches its command and that a case covers it, and CI runs that case.
acceptance_criteria: The doctrine is declared in the registry with its validator, and doctor fails if either half is missing
An adapter that applies a value the mapping does not derive is refused, and the refusal names the doctrine
A case covers the refusal and CI runs it
issues.risk: A blocking doctrine over a provider-specific adapter can refuse work in a repository whose provider changed underneath it; whether it blocks or advises is decided against that, and recorded.

issues.title: Publish the runtime-adapters claim with the test that proves it and the limits it does not cover
non_scope: Any behaviour change
Widening the claim beyond the limits an adapter applies
issues.objective: Move the runtime-adapters row from planned to guaranteed, citing the adapter and the case, and state on its detail page which axes remain advisory and why, so that the guarantee is narrower than the milestone title rather than as wide as it.
issues.why: A claim promoted to the width of its milestone title overstates what one adapter does. The matrix is where the difference between what is enforced and what is described is either kept honest or lost.
issues.current_state: The claim is planned, with no implementation and no test, and its note describes the rolled-back attempt.
issues.desired_state: The claim is guaranteed for the limits that are actually applied, names the file and the case, and says plainly which axes are still advice.
acceptance_criteria: The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist
The detail page names the axes that remain advisory
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: This is the moment the repository starts being believed about runtime enforcement; a claim wider than the adapter is worse than no claim.

issues.title: Define the execution record, including what an absence looks like
non_scope: Collecting anything; this issue defines what would be stored
Any field the tool would have to estimate to populate
issues.objective: Define the durable shape of a task's execution facts: which fields exist, who reported each one, and how a provider that reported nothing is recorded, so that absence is a value with a reason rather than a missing key or a zero.
issues.why: Every economic statement this repository could make rests on this record. If absence is representable only as a gap, the first report that reads it will treat a gap as a zero and the whole layer becomes an estimate wearing a measurement's clothes.
issues.current_state: Nothing measures a session. The economics document states what measurement would take and deliberately claims nothing, and no schema exists to be filled.
issues.desired_state: One schema, with an allowlist like every other record here, in which each measured field names its reporter, and not_reported is a first-class value carrying why it is absent.
acceptance_criteria: Every field names the reporter it came from, and a record without a reporter is refused
not_reported is representable with a reason, and is distinguishable from zero everywhere it is read
Unknown keys are refused like every other record in this repository
The schema is documented where the other file formats are
issues.risk: A schema designed around one provider's numbers becomes that provider's schema; the reporter field is what keeps a second provider from having to lie to fit.

issues.title: Record telemetry a provider reports, and refuse anything it did not
non_scope: Any network call, poll, or background collection
Deriving one field from another to fill a gap
issues.objective: Add the command that attaches measured execution facts to the active task, accepting only values a provider actually reported and refusing any field the caller cannot attribute to a reporter.
issues.why: The tool never invokes a model, so it cannot measure a session itself; the numbers have to be handed to it. The boundary where they arrive is the only place their provenance can still be checked.
issues.current_state: The record has a shape and nothing writes one.
issues.desired_state: A worker or a wrapper hands measured facts to one command, they are validated and stored against the task, and a value with no reporter is refused with a finding that names the field.
acceptance_criteria: Measured facts attach to the active task and survive into the completed record
A field without a reporter, or with a reporter that is not named, is refused
No code path fabricates, interpolates or defaults a measured value
The command works with no network and leaves no background process
issues.risk: A provider's self-reported usage may itself be wrong; the record says who reported it so that a later correction has something to correct.

issues.title: Prove a silent provider produces an explicit absence, never a guess
non_scope: Any change to the recording path; if the case fails, the fix belongs to the issue that owns that code
issues.objective: Write the case that runs a whole task under a provider that reports nothing and asserts that the completed record carries an explicit absence with a reason, and that no field anywhere in the surfaces shows an estimated number.
issues.why: The failure this milestone exists to avoid is not a missing feature, it is a plausible number nobody measured. Only a case that looks for the absence can keep that from creeping back in through a convenience default.
issues.current_state: The recording path exists. What happens when nobody reports anything is untested.
issues.desired_state: A case demonstrates the silent path end to end, and a grep-like assertion over the reporting surfaces shows no estimated value is ever printed as measured.
acceptance_criteria: The case runs start to finish with no telemetry reported and reaches a completed outcome
The stored record carries not_reported with a reason naming the provider
No surface prints a number for a task that reported none
issues.risk: A case that only checks the stored file misses a surface that fills a gap on its way to the screen; it has to assert on what is printed as well.

issues.title: Read the measurements back through the history surface, under a bound
non_scope: Aggregation, averages or any figure derived across tasks; that is the next milestone
issues.objective: Make recorded execution facts readable through the surface that already answers questions about past tasks, with the same retention bound the other durable stores carry.
issues.why: A measurement that can only be read by opening a file is a measurement nobody reads. It also has to be bounded, because an unbounded append-only store is exactly what this repository refuses everywhere else.
issues.current_state: Facts are recorded against tasks and can be read only from the record itself.
issues.desired_state: History reports the measured facts alongside the task they belong to, says not_reported where that is what happened, and the store is capped like the ledger.
acceptance_criteria: History shows measured facts and explicit absences for past tasks
The store has a declared retention bound and the bound is enforced by a case
No aggregate figure appears at this layer
issues.risk: Showing per-task numbers invites reading a trend into them; the surface has to present facts without implying a series.

issues.title: Publish the telemetry claim and record what remains unmeasured
non_scope: Any figure derived from the measurements
issues.objective: Move the telemetry claim to guaranteed for the providers that report honestly, name the implementation and the case, and state in the economics document which providers report nothing and what that costs the analysis.
issues.why: The value of this milestone is as much in what it refuses to claim as in what it measures. A reader has to be able to see which sessions are measured and which are not before believing any number built on top.
issues.current_state: The claim is planned and the economics document claims nothing on purpose.
issues.desired_state: The claim is guaranteed with its narrow scope stated, and the economics document says which providers are measured, which are not, and what follows from that.
acceptance_criteria: The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist
The economics document names the measured and unmeasured cases
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: Publishing measurement invites treating partial coverage as full coverage; the coverage statement has to sit next to the claim, not in a footnote.

issues.title: Define an accepted outcome, and join it to its measurements without storing the join
non_scope: Any stored aggregate
Counting a completed finish that the contract did not accept
issues.objective: Define precisely which finishes count as accepted outcomes, and derive the join between an accepted outcome and the execution facts of the work that produced it from records that already exist, storing no third record.
issues.why: Cost per outcome is a ratio, and both halves of it are already recorded: the finish contract decides acceptance and telemetry measures consumption. Storing the join would be a third place for them to disagree.
issues.current_state: The finish contract evaluates acceptance and records the outcome. Telemetry records what a session consumed. Nothing connects them, and the word outcome is used loosely across the documents.
issues.desired_state: One written definition of an accepted outcome, matching what the finish contract actually enforces, and a derivation that produces the set of accepted outcomes with their measurements, computed on demand.
acceptance_criteria: The definition matches what the finish contract enforces, and a case fails if the two drift apart
The join is derived from existing records, with nothing new persisted
An outcome whose work reported no telemetry appears in the set with an explicit absence
issues.risk: The tempting definition is the one that produces more data points; the correct one is the one the finish contract already enforces, even when that is a smaller set.

issues.title: Report cost only where measurement and acceptance both exist
non_scope: Elapsed time or token count used as a proxy for progress
Any projection of a future cost
issues.objective: Add the command that reports what accepted outcomes cost, computed only from measured facts, and reports no figure at all where either half is missing, saying which half.
issues.why: A cost report that fills gaps is worse than no cost report, because it is believed. The command has to be as willing to answer nothing as to answer a number.
issues.current_state: The join exists as a derivation. Nothing reports it.
issues.desired_state: One command answers what an accepted outcome cost, in text and as JSON, and where it cannot answer, it names whether acceptance or measurement was missing.
acceptance_criteria: A figure is reported only where a measured record and an accepted outcome both exist
Where no figure is reported, the output names which half was missing
JSON and text agree on the set of outcomes and the figures reported
issues.risk: The first number this command prints will be quoted somewhere; its units and its denominator have to be in the output itself, not only in the documentation.

issues.title: Make a thin denominator say so rather than average it away
non_scope: A confidence interval or any statistical model beyond stating the denominator
issues.objective: Make every reported figure carry the number of accepted outcomes it rests on, refuse to present a single observation as an average, and prove both with cases.
issues.why: Early on there will be very few accepted outcomes, and a mean over one of them looks exactly like a mean over many. The report has to make the difference impossible to miss.
issues.current_state: The command reports figures from whatever measured, accepted outcomes exist, however few.
issues.desired_state: Each figure states its denominator, and below the threshold the output presents observations rather than a summary statistic.
acceptance_criteria: Every reported figure carries the count of accepted outcomes behind it
Below the declared threshold the output presents observations and no average
The threshold is declared as data, not written into the code path
Cases cover the thin case and the sufficient case
issues.risk: Any threshold is arbitrary; declaring it as data and printing it beside the figure is what keeps it honest rather than hidden.

issues.title: Publish the cost-per-outcome claim with its unit defined beside it
non_scope: Any comparison against another tool or another team
issues.objective: Move the cost-per-outcome claim to guaranteed, define the unit and the denominator where a reader meets the figure, and state what the number cannot be used to compare.
issues.why: Cost per accepted outcome is the one figure this project argues is the right unit. Publishing it without saying what it excludes would repeat the mistake the economics document was written to avoid.
issues.current_state: The claim is planned. The economics document argues for the unit and reports nothing.
issues.desired_state: The claim is guaranteed, the unit and denominator are defined next to the reported figure, and the limits of comparison are stated.
acceptance_criteria: The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist
The unit and denominator are defined where the figure is presented
The document states what the figure cannot be used to compare
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: A published cost figure is the most quotable thing this repository will produce and the most easily stripped of its qualifiers.

issues.title: Group comparable work from what the records already carry
non_scope: A hand-written taxonomy of task types
Any new noun; the grouping is a derivation, not a record
issues.objective: Derive the grouping that makes two pieces of work comparable from facts the records already hold, so that a recommendation compares like with like without anybody inventing a taxonomy of task types.
issues.why: A recommendation is only meaningful within a class of comparable work, and the obvious way to get one is to invent categories. Invented categories are a new vocabulary nobody validates, which this repository refuses on principle and would regret in practice.
issues.current_state: Records carry a profile, a declared scope, a verification result and an outcome. Nothing groups them, and nothing says what makes two tasks comparable.
issues.desired_state: A derivation produces groups from recorded facts alone, states what it grouped on, and refuses to group where the facts are too thin to support it.
acceptance_criteria: Grouping uses only fields already recorded, and names them in its output
No new record type or vocabulary is introduced
Work that cannot be grouped is reported as ungrouped rather than forced into a group
issues.risk: A grouping that is too coarse makes every recommendation the same one; too fine and no group ever reaches a usable denominator. Whichever is chosen has to be visible in the output.

issues.title: Recommend a profile from measured cost, naming the measurements
non_scope: Invoking a model, or choosing a provider on a worker's behalf
issues.objective: Add the command that recommends a profile for a class of work from measured cost per accepted outcome, and prints the measurements the recommendation was derived from alongside it.
issues.why: A recommendation whose basis is not printed is an opinion with a command around it. Naming the measurements is what makes it checkable, and being checkable is the only thing that separates this from advice.
issues.current_state: Cost per accepted outcome is reported per outcome. Nothing recommends anything.
issues.desired_state: Asking which profile a class of work should use returns a profile, the measurements behind it, and the group they came from.
acceptance_criteria: Every recommendation lists the accepted outcomes and figures it was derived from
The recommendation names the group and how the group was derived
The command reads records and computes nothing that the cost layer already computes
issues.risk: Following a recommendation produces the data that justifies it; the output has to record that the measurements postdate earlier recommendations.

issues.title: Return no recommendation where the data is too thin, and say why
non_scope: A weaker recommendation with a caveat attached
issues.objective: Make insufficient data produce no recommendation rather than a weak one, with the threshold declared as data and the reason printed, proved by cases on both sides of it.
issues.why: The failure mode of every routing feature is a confident answer from three data points. Refusing to answer is the behaviour that has to be tested, because it is the one that will be pressured away.
issues.current_state: The command recommends from whatever measurements exist.
issues.desired_state: Below the threshold the command returns no recommendation and names what it would take to have one; above it, the recommendation carries its denominator.
acceptance_criteria: The threshold is declared as data and printed with every answer and every refusal
Below it, no profile is named at all
Cases cover both sides of the threshold
issues.risk: A threshold nobody can reach makes the whole command dead code; if the case shows the bar is unreachable in practice, that is a finding about the milestone, not a reason to lower it quietly.

issues.title: Prove the recommendation is advisory and publish it as such
non_scope: Any automatic application of a recommendation, behind a flag or otherwise
issues.objective: Prove with a case that a recommendation never changes the profile a task runs under, and publish the routing claim stating that Majordomus recommends and does not route.
issues.why: The distance between recommending a profile and selecting one is one convenience commit wide. A case is the only thing that keeps it, and the claim is where a reader is told which side of the line the tool is on.
issues.current_state: The command answers with a profile and a basis. Nothing proves it cannot act on its own answer.
issues.desired_state: A case starts a task after a recommendation and shows the profile is whatever the worker asked for, and the claim says recommendations only.
acceptance_criteria: A case shows a task starting under a profile different from the recommended one, unimpeded
The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist and says recommendations only
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: A tool that recommends is one flag away from a tool that decides; the case is the record of the decision not to add the flag.

issues.title: Let a policy name a shared source it does not copy
non_scope: Fetching a policy over a network, from a registry, or from any service
A hosted component that must be running for the tool to work
issues.objective: Let a repository's policy name a shared policy source and resolve it offline from the filesystem, so that one statement of a rule can govern more than one repository without being pasted into each.
issues.why: Copying is what makes organisational policy drift: every repository holds a fork of the rule and nobody can see which forks moved. A named source is the smallest change that makes drift detectable at all.
issues.current_state: Policy is per repository and entirely local. Nothing refers to anything outside the checkout.
issues.desired_state: A policy names a shared source, the tool resolves it without a network call, and every command that reads policy reads the resolved result.
acceptance_criteria: A shared source is resolved from the filesystem with no network access
Every policy reader sees the resolved policy, and no reader bypasses resolution
An unresolvable source is a named finding that stops the command, never a silent fallback to local
A repository that names no shared source behaves exactly as it does today
issues.risk: This is where a local-first tool grows a dependency outside its checkout; keeping resolution to the filesystem is what preserves the offline guarantee.

issues.title: Make a local override explicit and prove it survives an update of the shared source
non_scope: Overriding a rule the shared policy declares non-overridable, if such a class is introduced later
issues.objective: Define how a repository overrides part of a shared policy, require the override to be declared rather than inferred from a value differing, and prove with a case that updating the shared source leaves the override standing.
issues.why: An override that looks like an ordinary key is indistinguishable from a stale copy. Declaring it is what lets the drift report tell a deliberate exception from an accident.
issues.current_state: A shared source can be named and resolved. Anything a repository writes locally either wins or loses by a rule nobody has written down.
issues.desired_state: Overrides are declared, the merge order is documented and tested, and a shared source that changes underneath a repository does not silently take an override away.
acceptance_criteria: An override is a declaration, and a local value that differs without one is a finding
The merge order is documented and covered by a case
A case updates the shared source and shows the override still applies
issues.risk: Merge semantics are where shared configuration usually becomes unexplainable; the documented order and its case are the whole defence.

issues.title: Report drift from the shared policy in one command
non_scope: Changing anybody's policy; the command reports and never writes
issues.objective: Report, in one command, every way a repository's effective policy differs from the shared source it names, separating declared overrides from undeclared divergence.
issues.why: The point of naming a shared source is being able to see where it is not being followed. Without one command that answers that, shared policy is just a longer path to the same drift.
issues.current_state: A shared source is resolved and overrides are declared. Nothing summarises the difference.
issues.desired_state: One command lists each difference, says whether it is a declared override or undeclared divergence, and names the reproduce command for each.
acceptance_criteria: Every difference is listed with the key, both values, and whether it is declared
Undeclared divergence exits non-zero and declared overrides do not
Every finding carries a reproduce command
The command writes nothing
issues.risk: A drift report that is noisy is a drift report nobody runs; declared overrides have to be quiet by default.

issues.title: Prove the offline guarantee survives sharing
non_scope: Any offline cache of a remote source, which would be a fetch with extra steps
issues.objective: Prove with cases and a doctrine that no path introduced by shared policy reaches a network, and that an unavailable shared source degrades to a named refusal rather than a fetch or a silent local fallback.
issues.why: Every guarantee this tool makes rests on it being local and offline. Sharing policy across repositories is the exact feature that historically converts a local tool into a client of something, and it has to be refused structurally rather than by intention.
issues.current_state: Resolution, override and drift reporting all exist and are documented as filesystem-only. Nothing enforces that they stay so.
issues.desired_state: A doctrine refuses a network call in the policy resolution path, cases cover an unavailable source, and the refusal names the doctrine.
acceptance_criteria: A doctrine declares the rule, its validator exists, and doctor proves it reaches the command that runs it
A case shows an unavailable shared source producing a named refusal, with nothing fetched and no fallback
CI runs the case
issues.risk: The pressure to add a remote source arrives with the first user who has repositories on two machines; the doctrine is what makes that a decision rather than a patch.

issues.title: Publish the shared-policy claim and what sharing still cannot do
non_scope: Any claim about repositories that have not adopted the shared source
issues.objective: Move the shared-policy claim to guaranteed, cite the implementation and the cases, and state plainly what a shared policy does not provide: no service, no registry, no cross-machine visibility, and no enforcement of a repository that never adopts it.
issues.why: Shared policy is the version most easily read as an organisational control plane. The claim has to name the boundary in the same place it names the capability, or the boundary will be assumed away.
issues.current_state: The claim is planned, and the design document places multi-repository policy outside the local-first scope with a note that it returns here.
issues.desired_state: The claim is guaranteed for what is implemented, the limitations page names what it is not, and the design document's deferral is reconciled with what now exists.
acceptance_criteria: The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist
The limitations page names what shared policy does not do
The design document no longer defers what has shipped, and still refuses what has not
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: This claim is the one a reader will most want to be wider than it is.

issues.title: Reproduce the misattribution as an executable case
non_scope: Any change to lib/decision.sh, lib/checkpoint.sh or lib/question.sh
issues.objective: Write a behavioural case in which two workers share one checkout — one starts a task, the other records a decision — and assert what happens today, so that the defect stops being an anecdote and becomes something a command demonstrates.
issues.why: This was found by three sessions colliding in one evening, which is a story rather than a test. A characterisation case is what makes the fix provable and what turns the eventual behaviour change red if it regresses.
issues.current_state: decision, checkpoint and question resolve the active task from .majordomus/state/current.yaml. Nothing in test/cases exercises a second worker writing while somebody else's task is active.
issues.desired_state: A case runs the sequence in a disposable repository, asserts that the record is attributed to the active task rather than to the worker that wrote it, and says in a comment that this is the gap being characterised rather than the behaviour being blessed.
acceptance_criteria: The case starts a task, then records a decision as a second worker, and reaches an entry in decisions.md
It asserts the current attribution explicitly and marks it in a comment as the gap, not the goal
It covers checkpoint and question as well as decision, or says why they are out of its reach
It runs in a disposable repository like every other case
issues.risk: A characterisation test that pins the wrong behaviour is a trap unless the comment saying so is unmissable; that comment is the whole safety mechanism.

issues.title: Decide how a record is attributed, between named alternatives
non_scope: Implementing anything
issues.objective: Choose between the alternatives that actually exist — attribute to the session that ran the command, refuse to write when the active task belongs to somebody else, or require the task to be named explicitly — and record the choice with the case each rejected option gets wrong.
issues.why: Every option here trades a different thing away, and the wrong one either invents an identity this repository refuses to maintain or makes the common single-worker case tedious. A decision record is the only artefact that survives to explain why the chosen one was chosen.
issues.current_state: The gap is reproduced. Nothing has been decided, and the obvious fix — a worker identity the tool maintains — is the one the doctrine against new nouns exists to prevent.
issues.desired_state: One decision record naming the choice, both rejected alternatives, and the situation each of them is wrong in, with the conditions the choice imposes on the implementation.
acceptance_criteria: The record names the choice and both rejected alternatives, each with the case it gets wrong
Any identity the choice relies on is supplied by the session and stored only inside the record it explains
The conditions the implementation must meet are stated, not left to the implementer
issues.risk: Choosing to refuse rather than to attribute makes a single worker pay for a problem only concurrent workers have; whichever way it goes, the cost falls on somebody and the record has to say who.

issues.title: Implement the decision and prove it holds
non_scope: Any behaviour the decision did not choose
issues.objective: Implement whatever I0702 decided across every command that writes a durable record, and turn the characterisation case into one that asserts the new behaviour.
issues.why: A defect is fixed when the case that reproduced it goes from describing the gap to describing the guarantee. Anything less leaves the next worker unable to tell which of the two the code is in.
issues.current_state: The choice is recorded. decision, checkpoint and question still resolve the active task from the checkout, and the case still asserts that.
issues.desired_state: Every command that writes a durable record follows the decision, the case asserts the new behaviour, and a refusal — if that is what was chosen — names the rule that refused and what to run instead.
acceptance_criteria: Every command that writes a durable record is covered, not only decision
The case from I0701 asserts the guarantee rather than the gap
A refusal names the rule and the command that resolves it
If the rule is enforced, it is declared in share/doctrines.yaml and doctor proves it reaches its command
issues.risk: Three commands share this resolution path; fixing one and not the others leaves a defect that looks fixed, which is worse than one that looks broken.

issues.title: Publish what attribution guarantees, and what it still cannot
non_scope: Any behaviour change
Any claim about verifying who a worker is
issues.objective: State on the public surface what a record's attribution now means, and state plainly what it does not: that a worker's identity is supplied by the session, not verified, and that nothing here proves who a worker was.
issues.why: Attribution is the kind of guarantee a reader will assume is stronger than it is. The distance between naming a worker and authenticating one has to be written where the claim is, not left to be inferred.
issues.current_state: The behaviour will exist and be tested. Nothing on the public surface says what it covers.
issues.desired_state: A claim states what is guaranteed with the file and the case behind it, and says on its detail page that the identity is asserted by the session and never verified.
acceptance_criteria: The claim cites an implementation path and a test path that both exist
The detail page says the identity is supplied, not verified
The generated site data regenerates with no stale file
issues.risk: A claim about attribution read as a claim about authentication would be the most damaging overstatement on the site.

issues.title: Narrow the Clean Extraction Boundary and record what was adopted
non_scope: Any implementation
Any change to the ten items already recorded as having crossed the boundary
Naming any internal path, component or vocabulary of the studied material
issues.objective: Rewrite the Clean Extraction Boundary in docs/DESIGN.md so that it permits a generic deterministic provenance graph derived from this repository's own artifacts while continuing to exclude everything it excludes today, and record in docs/EXTRACTION_REPORT.md which architectural ideas from the studied prior art were adopted by re-derivation and which were refused, each with its reason.
issues.why: The boundary currently reads 'graph semantics' among the things excluded absolutely. The rest of this milestone builds a reference graph. Shipping that against a published boundary that forbids it would make the boundary decorative, which is precisely the failure mode this project was built to detect. The adoption record exists so that the next reader can tell a re-derived idea from a copied implementation.
issues.current_state: docs/DESIGN.md lists 'graph semantics' in the absolute exclusion sentence and lists ten items that crossed the boundary by abstraction. docs/EXTRACTION_REPORT.md records the evidence behind the v0.1 decisions and says nothing about session or knowledge tooling.
issues.desired_state: The exclusion sentence distinguishes the domain, inference and semantic machinery that stays out from the generic provenance graph over this repository's own files that is now in. The adopted list names the session and knowledge ideas taken by re-derivation. A refusal list names what was studied and deliberately not taken, each with the reason, including the database, the embedding layer, the vault renderer and the copied-narrative session note.
acceptance_criteria: The boundary states what kind of graph is permitted and what kind is still excluded, in one sentence a reader can apply to a proposed feature
The adoption list names each adopted idea and the Majordomus object it becomes
The refusal list names each refused idea and why, with the databases and the embedding layer among them
No internal path, hostname, component name or quotation from the studied material appears anywhere in either document

evidence.result: exit 0, and test case 08_no_forbidden_constructs passes alongside it. The boundary now states a provenance test a reader can apply to a proposal: an edge that can name the line stating it is a reference, one that exists because something looked related is a semantic claim and stays out. Section 11 of the extraction report records the second-pass evidence, seventeen adopted ideas with the object each becomes here, and eleven refusals including every database, embeddings, generated summaries and a note-vault renderer

issues.risk: A boundary narrowed to fit the feature being built is not a boundary. The wording has to be one a reader could use to refuse a future proposal, not one that merely describes what is about to be committed.

issues.title: Specify the session record before writing one
non_scope: Any implementation
The knowledge layer
Retention policy, which its own issue settles
issues.objective: Define the session object in docs/SCHEMAS.md and docs/CONTINUITY.md: what a session is, how it differs from a task and from a handover, the filename grammar of a closed record, the exact field list, which fields are computed from git, and the rule that the reference envelope is derived rather than accumulated.
issues.why: Every other issue in this milestone writes or reads that file. Specifying it after implementing it is how a schema ends up describing one caller. The distinction that has to survive is the one the whole milestone rests on: a task is a unit of work, a session is an execution episode, and a handover is a deliberate package for whoever continues — three objects that are easy and expensive to conflate.
issues.current_state: docs/CONTINUITY.md names six kinds of durable record and no session among them. docs/SCHEMAS.md documents current.yaml, the checkpoint and handover record shape, decisions.md, open-questions.md and the ledger.
issues.desired_state: The session is the seventh kind, documented beside the others, with its mutable active record and its immutable closed record described separately, its field list given, and the derivation rule stated: the tasks, issues, checkpoints, handovers, decisions and questions of an episode are read out of the ledger between the session's own timestamps, never written into the session file by another command.
acceptance_criteria: The three-way distinction between task, session and handover is stated with the case each one gets wrong if conflated
The closed record's filename grammar is given and shown to be lexicographically chronological, branch-safe and collision-safe
Every field is listed with its source, and the computed ones are marked as never authored
The derivation rule is stated, with the alternative it rejects and why

evidence.result: exit 0. CONCEPTS.md gains session and envelope to the vocabulary and a section naming what each of the three possible collapses loses; SCHEMAS.md documents the open record and the immutable closed record with the full field list, the filename grammar and the four properties it carries, and a table giving the identity used for each reference kind with the two weak ones marked as weak; CONTINUITY.md adds the seventh kind, the envelope-not-narrative rule, the derivation rule with the rejected alternative, and what a session is not

issues.risk: A schema written before the implementation can specify something the portable-shell floor cannot express. Each field has to be one that git, the ledger or a single-line YAML scalar can carry.

issues.title: Open a session and report its status
non_scope: Closing a session
Any reading of the ledger
Knowledge
issues.objective: Implement lib/session.sh with `session start` and `session status`: one active session per worktree in .majordomus/state/session-current.yaml, its identity and git facts computed, a second start refused rather than silently replacing the first, and a status that reports the active session against current git or says plainly that none is open.
issues.why: The active record is the anchor every later command reads. It has to refuse rather than overwrite, because an execution episode that silently replaces another one loses the boundary the whole object exists to draw.
issues.current_state: There is no session command and no session state file. bin/majordomus dispatches its subcommands from a fixed case list.
issues.desired_state: `majordomus session start` writes the active record atomically at mode 0600, records session_id, started_at, owner, an optionally supplied worker identity, and the computed repository_id, worktree, branch, start_head and start_working_tree. It refuses when a session is already open in this worktree and names the command that closes it. `session status` prints the open session with its divergence label, or reports absence. Both are dispatched from bin/majordomus and appear in its usage.
acceptance_criteria: The command has a section in docs/CLI.md, because the site generator refuses a dispatched command with none, and it documents only what is implemented
A session starts, the active record exists, and its identity fields match git
A second start is refused with a non-zero exit and names the closing command
A session started in one worktree does not appear as active in another
status reports absence as absence rather than as an error
The active record's unknown keys are rejected by an allowlist like every other Majordomus YAML file

evidence.result: 1 passed. The case proves identity is computed from git rather than authored, that absence is answered as absence and exit 0, that the record is mode 0600, that an unsupplied worker stays unrecorded rather than being invented, that a second open is refused with exit 15 and names the closing command, that a record whose worktree is another checkout is reported and does not block this one, that a corrupt record exits 10 rather than being read as no session, and that status writes nothing. The repository shellcheck gate passes at warning severity over the whole tree

issues.risk: One active session per worktree is the same rule current.yaml already has, and current.yaml is tracked, so it travels with the branch and appears active in a checkout that never started it. The session record has to record its worktree and be read with the same foreign-record rule.

issues.title: Close a session into an envelope derived from the ledger
non_scope: Reading a closed record back, which is its own issue
Retention and archiving
Any copying of a checkpoint, handover or decision body into the session file
issues.objective: Implement `session close`: read the active record, derive the episode's references from the ledger between its start and now, write an immutable closed record with computed end-state git facts and an optional authored summary body, remove the active record, and append the close event to the ledger.
issues.why: This is the mechanism that makes the session an envelope rather than a narrative. Nothing accumulates references during the episode, so no command outside session pays for them; and because the ledger is append-only and machine-written, the envelope is a derivation of existing evidence rather than a second account of it.
issues.current_state: The ledger records task, checkpoint, handover, finish, decision, question, plan and maintenance events, each with a timestamp, a branch and a head. Nothing reads a time range out of it.
issues.desired_state: A closed record under .majordomus/state/sessions/ carries the computed identity, started_at and closed_at, start and end head and working tree, the outcome, and reference lists of task ids, issue ids, milestone ids, checkpoint paths, handover paths, decision entries and question ids observed in the ledger window. It copies no body. An authored summary on stdin is optional and is stored as the record body, subject to the identity-field refusal every other record uses.
acceptance_criteria: Closing writes an immutable record, removes the active record, and appends one ledger event
The reference lists match the events the ledger holds in the window, and nothing outside the window appears
An episode that spans two tasks names both; a task that spans two sessions is named by both
No body of any referenced record appears in the session file, and a case asserts that
An authored summary containing an identity field is refused, as it is for a checkpoint
issues.risk: The ledger window is bounded by timestamps with second resolution, so two episodes that abut within one second could each claim an event. The ledger's line order is the existing tiebreak for exactly this and has to be used rather than the timestamps alone.

issues.title: Read sessions back with a divergence label
non_scope: Knowledge
Any repository-wide resolution across worktrees
issues.objective: Implement `session list`, `session show <id>` and `session latest`, each resolving with the established rule — same repository, same worktree, same branch, then same branch — and each printing the existing divergence label of the record against current git.
issues.why: A closed session from a rewritten branch that is presented as current knowledge is the failure the divergence vocabulary already exists to prevent. Reusing that vocabulary rather than inventing a second one is the whole point of having it.
issues.current_state: mj_resolve_latest implements the two-tier rule for checkpoints and handovers, and mj_git_label produces exact, advanced, diverged and different_context. No command reads a session.
issues.desired_state: list prints sessions newest first with their labels; show prints one record whole; latest prints the newest session that resolves for this worktree and branch, and reports absence as absence. A diverged or different_context record is labelled as such on every one of them.
acceptance_criteria: Sessions list in chronological order, and the order is not taken from file modification time
Two sessions written inside the same second order deterministically
A record whose recorded head is not an ancestor of HEAD is labelled diverged wherever it is printed
A session from another branch is never offered as latest
Every one of these commands leaves git status byte-identical
issues.risk: Reusing mj_resolve_latest requires the session record to have the same front-matter shape as a checkpoint. If the record is pure YAML instead, a second resolver appears, and two resolution rules is exactly the thing the resolution section of the documentation refuses.

issues.title: Make the session rules doctrines, with retention and archiving
non_scope: Any background or automatic maintenance
Deleting a record under any circumstance
issues.objective: Declare the session rules in share/doctrines.yaml with validators that doctor and watch dispatch — a malformed active or closed record, a session left open past its policy, a reference to a record that does not exist, and retention over the declared cap — and implement policy-driven archiving that never deletes and never overwrites.
issues.why: A rule enforced by an inline check in one command is the declared-but-not-wired failure this tool measures in other people's repositories. Every enforced rule here is declared in the registry and dispatched from it, or it is not enforced.
issues.current_state: The doctrine registry declares every enforced rule with a validator, the commands that dispatch it, a claim and a test. history --rotate is the existing precedent for retention that archives rather than deletes and refuses to overwrite an existing archive.
issues.desired_state: session_record_integrity and session_reference_integrity are declared and dispatched. The policy carries a session block with the retention cap and whether archiving is enabled, its keys are in the policy allowlist, and retention_caps reports sessions alongside checkpoints and handovers. Archiving happens only when a command asks for it.
acceptance_criteria: Both doctrines appear in doctrine list with a validator that exists, and doctor proves each reaches the command that claims to run it
A malformed closed record fails doctor and drifts watch, and the finding carries a reproduce command
A session naming a checkpoint path that does not exist is reported, naming both
Archiving moves records without deleting them and refuses to overwrite an existing archive
A session left open longer than the policy allows is reported by watch and does not block anything
issues.risk: An open session is normal for most of its life, so the staleness rule has to be advisory. A blocking check on an open session would refuse work during the episode it is meant to describe.

issues.title: Discover knowledge sources from git, not from the filesystem
non_scope: Extraction, nodes, edges
Any recursive walk of a hidden directory
Indexing a path merely because it exists
issues.objective: Implement the discovery stage of lib/knowledge.sh: a declared list of source classes, each with a scope of shared or operational, resolved through git ls-files for tracked repository artifacts and through the known state paths for operational records, producing a deterministic ordered list of sources with their content hashes.
issues.why: A recursive filesystem walk indexes vendored trees, build output, editor droppings and untracked files that were never meant to be knowledge, and it produces a different answer on two machines. git ls-files answers with repository truth, in a stable order, and is already the boundary this project treats as authoritative.
issues.current_state: Nothing in lib/ enumerates repository files. scripts/generate-site-data declares its canonical inputs, which is the precedent for a declared source list rather than a walk.
issues.desired_state: `knowledge sources` prints each discovered source with its class, its scope and its hash, in a deterministic order, and the same repository produces the same list twice. An untracked file is not a source. Operational state paths are added explicitly and are marked operational, never shared.
acceptance_criteria: The source classes are declared in one place and each carries its scope
Discovery is driven by git for tracked sources, and a case proves an untracked file is excluded
The output order is deterministic and independent of filesystem order
A pathname containing a space or a non-ASCII character is handled without splitting
A declared source class that discovers nothing is reported, so a forgotten path is visible

evidence.result: 1 passed, and the four cases the new command affected — 15_command_surface, 26_ci_wiring, 28_no_hardcoded_values, 51_derived_artifacts_committed — pass with it. The case proves an untracked file is never a source, that vendored and built trees are excluded because they are not tracked, that two runs agree and a touched file does not reorder them, that editing one source changes only its own hash, that a pathname with spaces and non-ASCII characters yields exactly one row, that no file is discovered by two classes, that a required class discovering nothing is a WARN, and that every read leaves the working tree byte-identical

issues.risk: The historical whitespace bug class lives here. Every pathname read out of git has to be read NUL-safely or with an explicit field separator, never through unquoted word splitting.

issues.title: Extract nodes with identities that survive a rebuild
non_scope: Edges
The manifest
Any full Markdown parser
issues.objective: Implement the extract and normalise stages in lib/knowledge.awk: one node per canonical object, with an identity derived from its canonical id or its repository path, a kind that is only asserted when a structural fact establishes it, and a title taken from the record or from the document's first heading.
issues.why: Identity is what makes the index a pointer rather than a copy. An id derived from enumeration order or from a title changes when something unrelated changes, and every reference to it silently becomes wrong. Classification that guesses from prose is the same failure in another dimension: a confident wrong kind is worse than an honest unknown.
issues.current_state: The canonical objects already have identities — claims, milestones, issues, profiles, prompts and doctrines are all keyed — and lib/project.awk is the precedent for deriving a model in awk from flattened records.
issues.desired_state: Nodes are emitted in a stable order with ids of the form kind and canonical key, where the key is the object's own id for structured records and its repository path for documents. A kind is asserted from the source class or from an explicit field, never from a keyword found in prose, and an unrecognised source yields the unknown kind rather than a guess.
acceptance_criteria: Two syncs of an unchanged repository produce byte-identical node output
Renaming a document changes that document's node id and no other
A node's kind comes from its source class or an explicit field, and a case proves prose containing a kind word does not change it
An unrecognisable source produces a node of kind unknown rather than being dropped or guessed at
Extraction from a generic Markdown document takes only the path, the first heading and explicit links
issues.risk: Deriving a document id from its path means a rename is a delete and an add, which is correct and will look like churn. The alternative, a content hash identity, makes an edit a delete and an add, which is worse.

issues.title: Record only edges that a file states, each with where it was observed
non_scope: Inferring a relationship from prose
Any similarity, clustering or taxonomy generation
Session edges, which arrive with the session integration
issues.objective: Implement the resolve and graph stages: edges derived from the explicit relationships the canonical files already declare — claim to source, implementation and test; issue to milestone and to its dependencies; evidence to issue; doctrine to validator, claim and test; record to task — each carrying the file and field it was observed in, and none carrying a relationship inferred from prose.
issues.why: The repository already contains a dense, hand-maintained, machine-readable graph that no command can traverse. Extracting it costs nothing in accuracy because every edge is stated. Heuristic extraction from prose would add edges nobody wrote, and an edge nobody wrote cannot be checked by the person who would notice it is wrong.
issues.current_state: docs/CLAIMS.yaml states three relationships per claim; the issue files state a milestone and a dependency list; share/doctrines.yaml states a validator, a claim list, a test and the commands that enforce it; every continuity record states its task. Nothing reads any of them as a graph.
issues.desired_state: An edge is a from, a to, a type and a provenance, and the graph stage rejects an edge missing any of the four. Edge types are a closed declared set. A dangling edge — one whose target is not a node — is retained and reported rather than dropped, because a broken reference is the finding.
acceptance_criteria: Every edge carries the source file it was observed in, and an edge without provenance is a validation failure rather than a silent drop
The edge types are a declared closed set and an undeclared type is an error
Changing a dependency in an issue file changes the graph on the next sync with no generated file edited by hand
A dangling edge is reported and names both ends
No edge is produced from a Markdown link whose target is outside the repository
issues.risk: Markdown links are the one edge source that is not curated. Treating a broken external link as the same severity as a broken claim-to-test reference would make a permanent red gate out of an intentional outbound link; ownership and severity have to be distinguished.

issues.title: A content-hash manifest that makes a second sync cheap
non_scope: Search
Any automatic rebuild triggered by a read
issues.objective: Implement the manifest: one row per source with its path, content hash, extractor version and the node ids it produced, written beside the generated graph, compared on every sync, and used so that a sync with no source change does no extraction and says so.
issues.why: Without a manifest, every query is tempted to rebuild and every rebuild is a full one. The manifest is what makes staleness detectable without mutating anything, which is what lets the read-only commands stay read-only.
issues.current_state: Nothing is generated and nothing is cached. The site generator's --check mode is the precedent for a command that reports drift between canonical input and derived output without regenerating it.
issues.desired_state: `knowledge sync` writes the manifest with the graph. `knowledge sync --check` compares source hashes against the manifest and exits non-zero when they differ, writing nothing. `knowledge status` reports fresh or stale and names the sources that moved. A no-op sync is measurably cheaper than a cold one, and the measurement is recorded.
acceptance_criteria: A second sync with no source change reports no work and leaves the generated files byte-identical
Editing one source changes that source's manifest row and the nodes derived from it, and no other row
sync --check writes nothing and exits non-zero when a source has moved
The extractor version is part of the manifest, so a change to the extractor invalidates it
The measured cost of a no-op sync and of a cold sync on this repository is recorded as evidence
issues.risk: If a no-op sync is not materially cheaper than a cold one, the manifest has failed and should be removed rather than kept as decoration. The measurement is the acceptance criterion, not the design.

issues.title: Read-only knowledge lookup with an ordering that can be explained
non_scope: Any change to the existing search command's behaviour
Embeddings, similarity, or any opaque score
Rebuilding the index from a read
issues.objective: Implement `knowledge search`, `knowledge show` and `knowledge related`: deterministic lookup over the generated index with a documented, tested match order, JSON output that names the field each result matched on, and no write of any kind.
issues.why: A query that rebuilds the index mutates the repository as a side effect of asking a question, which makes a read-only command a write and breaks every reproduce line that follows it. And a relevance order nobody can explain is one nobody can debug; the order has to be a rule, not a score.
issues.current_state: `majordomus search` is a literal grep over the six operational record kinds and must keep that contract unchanged. Nothing searches the repository's canonical artifacts.
issues.desired_state: `knowledge search` ranks by an explicit ladder — exact canonical id, exact title, title prefix, path, tag, then literal body match — and reports the matched field for every result. `knowledge show` prints one node with its source path and hash. `knowledge related` prints the edges into and out of one node with their provenance. A stale index is reported, never silently rebuilt.
acceptance_criteria: The match ladder is documented and a case asserts the order for a query that matches at two levels
JSON output carries the id, kind, title, source and matched field of every result
Running every read-only knowledge command leaves git status byte-identical
A stale index is reported as stale by every read command, and none of them rebuilds it
The existing search command's output and exit codes are unchanged, proved by its own case still passing
issues.risk: Two commands now contain the word search with different corpora and different contracts. If the distinction is not stated where a worker reads it, the wrong one gets used and the answer looks like an absence.

issues.title: Validate the graph, and let doctor and watch ask the same validator
non_scope: Repairing anything automatically
Failing on a link to a resource outside the repository
issues.objective: Implement `knowledge validate` detecting duplicate node ids, dangling explicit references, source paths that no longer exist, hash mismatches, edges with a missing end, edges without provenance and a stale generated index, each with a severity and a reproduce command, and declare the rule in the doctrine registry so doctor and watch dispatch the same validator rather than reimplementing it.
issues.why: Validation logic that exists twice diverges, and the second copy is the one that stops being run. The registry is the mechanism that makes doctor, watch and the command itself provably the same rule.
issues.current_state: Doctrines are declared with a validator, the commands that enforce it and its test; doctor proves each link of that chain from the source rather than from the declaration.
issues.desired_state: knowledge_integrity is declared and dispatched from doctor and watch. Findings distinguish a broken Majordomus-owned reference, which is a failure, from a broken link to a deliberately external resource, which is not. Doctor also answers whether the index can be built at all in this checkout.
acceptance_criteria: Every listed condition is detected by a case that introduces exactly that fault
The doctrine appears in doctrine list, doctor proves it reaches both commands, and its test is named
Severity distinguishes an owned reference from an external one, and the rule for which is which is stated
A stale index is drift under watch and a failure under the command, and neither rebuilds it
doctor reports whether the index is buildable here without leaving one behind
issues.risk: A validator that runs a full extraction inside doctor makes doctor slow enough to be skipped, and a check nobody runs is the failure this project measures. It has to compare hashes rather than rebuild.

issues.title: A closed session becomes a node that points at its episode
non_scope: Any inference about why a session touched something
Copying a session summary into a node
issues.objective: Extract closed sessions as knowledge nodes whose edges point at the tasks, issues, checkpoints, handovers, decisions and questions they name, so that the graph answers which sessions touched an issue, which decisions affected it, and which handover continued a task — without any session body being copied anywhere.
issues.why: This is what makes the two halves of the milestone one thing. Temporal and causal navigation is what a worker actually wants from a prior session, and it is exactly the part that does not require reading the prose.
issues.current_state: The knowledge graph covers repository artifacts. Sessions exist as records that nothing traverses.
issues.desired_state: A session node carries its id, its window and its outcome; its edges carry the relationship and the session record they were observed in. Checkpoints, which are numerous and individually low-value, are represented as references from the session rather than as one node each, so that a high-volume record kind does not dominate the graph.
acceptance_criteria: A query for an issue names the sessions that touched it, and each answer carries the session record it came from
A session node holds no body text from any record it references
A high-volume record kind does not produce one node per file where a reference list is sufficient, and the reason is stated
Sessions are operational scope and never shared, proved by a case
issues.risk: Every operational record kind added to the graph increases the chance one of them leaks into a shared projection. The scope field has to be the only thing that decides, and it has to be tested at the projection boundary rather than at each producer.

issues.title: Give the worker a bounded slice of knowledge, not the knowledge base
non_scope: Any similarity-based selection
Rebuilding the index from context
Raising the existing line budget
issues.objective: Add a knowledge section to `majordomus context`, selected deterministically from what the active task and issue already reference, capped by a profile toggle and an item limit, dropped before any immutable fact when the budget is short, and named under EXCLUDED whenever it is dropped or switched off.
issues.why: A context builder that dumps an index has replaced a selection problem with a bigger one. The value is in choosing the few pointers a worker needs, from relationships that are already explicit, and in saying out loud what was left out.
issues.current_state: context assembles nine sections in authority order with a fixed drop order and names every exclusion. Its profile toggles decide what is asked for.
issues.desired_state: The profile carries a knowledge toggle and a maximum item count, both in the profile allowlist. The section lists pointers — id, kind, title and source path — for the current issue, its dependencies, the claims it names and the documents it references. It sits below every immutable fact in the drop order and above nothing that outranks it.
acceptance_criteria: The section appears only when the profile asks for it, and its absence is named under EXCLUDED with the toggle that caused it
It is dropped before git, the task, the profile and open blockers under a tight budget, and the drop is named
Selection comes from explicit references only, and a case proves an unrelated document is not selected
A stale index makes the section report staleness rather than silently omit itself
The existing context case still passes unchanged
issues.risk: The budget is already close to full on a rich task. If the knowledge section is added without measuring, it will be the section that always gets dropped, which is a feature nobody receives.

issues.title: Say what is now true in the claims, the documentation and the worker instructions
non_scope: Any website change
A claim for a subcommand that has no behaviour of its own
issues.objective: Add the behavioural claims this milestone earns to docs/CLAIMS.yaml with real implementation and test paths, document the commands in docs/CLI.md, correct the sentence in docs/CONTINUITY.md that says no index is maintained, write docs/KNOWLEDGE.md, and extend the provider-neutral instruction source so a fresh worker knows the session and knowledge steps of the lifecycle.
issues.why: A capability with no claim is invisible, a claim with no test is the failure this project measures in other people's repositories, and a document that contradicts the code teaches the wrong thing to every worker that reads it.
issues.current_state: docs/CONTINUITY.md states that search maintains no index because the corpus is a handful of files, which describes the record corpus correctly and the repository corpus not at all. The instruction source describes the task lifecycle with no session step.
issues.desired_state: The distinction is stated: record search is a direct literal scan with no index, knowledge search is a derived index over a broader corpus, and neither outranks git or the canonical files. Claims name behaviour rather than subcommands. The worker instructions describe the loop from session start to session close, and teach retrieval of what is needed rather than reading the whole base.
acceptance_criteria: Every added claim has a source, an implementation and a test path that all exist, and no guaranteed claim lacks a test
docs/CONTINUITY.md distinguishes the two searches, and the old sentence no longer contradicts the code
The Clean Extraction Boundary and the continuity document agree with each other about the graph
The regenerated provider projections stay under the always-loaded budget
The instruction source teaches retrieval, not reading the whole base
issues.risk: The always-loaded budget is a hard cap with a failing check. Adding lifecycle steps to the instruction body can push it over, and the fix must be to say less rather than to raise the cap.

issues.title: Prove the loop on a real issue, without a transcript
non_scope: Any new capability
Any performance guarantee in README or claims that the measurement does not support
issues.objective: Execute the whole lifecycle against a real issue of this repository — session start, plan next, plan show, context, knowledge retrieval, work, checkpoint and decision, evidence, plan done, session close, knowledge sync, watch — and record as evidence what a following session could determine from the records alone.
issues.why: The milestone is not finished when a command returns something. It is finished when a worker with no conversation history can say what happened, why, what was decided, which evidence supports it, where the canonical source lives and what to do next. That is a demonstration, not an assertion, and it is the only acceptance criterion that tests the parts against each other.
issues.current_state: The pieces are individually tested in disposable repositories. Nothing has run the assembled loop on this repository's own canonical model.
issues.desired_state: The loop has been run, its measurements recorded — discovery, cold sync, no-op sync, search, context assembly — and the questions a following worker can answer from records alone are listed with the command that answers each.
acceptance_criteria: The loop ran on a real issue and the evidence names the commands and what each showed
Each of the six questions a following worker must answer is listed with the command that answers it
The measurements are recorded, and no number appears in README or claims that they do not support
A read-only pass over the whole surface leaves git status byte-identical
issues.risk: A dogfood run that is narrated rather than measured proves nothing. Every claim in the evidence has to name a command that produced it.

findings.subject: I0804
findings.message: shares test/cases with I0808; they may not run concurrently
